beats.say: Look at this equation. 2 x, plus 15, equals 29. Our job is to find the number that x stands for.

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 2 x has a plus 15 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: The two sides are level, like a see-saw. We want the 2 x on its own. What is in its way?
To undo plus 15, we take away 15. And to keep the balance level, we take it from both sides.
On the left, plus 15 and minus 15 cancel each other out. On the right, 29 minus 15 makes 14.

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: Nearly there. 2 x means 2 times x. What undoes times 2?
Divide by 2, then. The left side and the right side, both of them.
14 shared into 2 equal parts gives 7 each. So x equals 7.
Good mathematicians always check. Put 7 back in place of x. 2 times 7 is 14, and 14 plus 15 is 29. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added or taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Here is our equation. 3 x, minus 5, equals 4. A number is hiding behind that x, and we are going to find it.

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 3 x has a minus 5 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 3 x?
To undo minus 5, we add 5. And to keep the balance level, we add it to both sides.
On the left, minus 5 and plus 5 cancel each other out. On the right, 4 plus 5 makes 9.

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 3, we divide by 3.

beats.say: Now only the 3 is stuck to x. 3 x means 3 times x. So how do we undo times 3?
Divide by 3, then. The left side and the right side, both of them.
9 divided by 3 is 3. So x equals 3. There is our hidden number!
Let's make sure. Put 3 where the x was. 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 minus 5 is 4. It works.
Two undo steps, in order: first the number that is added or taken away, then the number that multiplies x. And always the same on both sides.
Look at this equation. 6 x, plus 11, equals 35. Our job is to find the number that x stands for.

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 6 x has a plus 11 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 6 x?
To undo plus 11, we take away 11. And to keep the balance level, we take it from both sides.
On the left, plus 11 and minus 11 cancel each other out. On the right, 35 minus 11 makes 24.

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 6, we divide by 6.

beats.say: Nearly there. 6 x means 6 times x. What undoes times 6?
So we divide both sides by 6. Careful: both sides, or the balance tips.
24 divided by 6 is 4. So x equals 4. We found it.
Now the check. Swap the x for 4 and see if the two sides agree. 6 times 4 is 24, and 24 plus 11 is 35. It works.
Remember the order. First undo the plus or minus, on both sides. Then divide, on both sides. That is the whole method.

board.text: Rectangle: one side 8 cm, perimeter 40 cm

beats.say: Here is a rectangle. One side is 8 centimetres and the perimeter is 40 centimetres. We want the area.
For the area we need both sides, and we only have one. The perimeter will give us the other. Remember, the perimeter is the walk all the way round: 2 lengths and 2 breadths.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth take us exactly halfway round. So it is half of 40. Dividing by 4 only works for a square.

beats.say: The whole walk is 40. So how far is just one length plus one breadth?
One length and one breadth are halfway round. Half of 40 is 20.
The two sides together make 20, and one of them is 8. So the other side is 20 take away 8, which is 12 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Area is the space inside, rows of little squares. So we multiply the length by the breadth. Adding is for the walk round the edge.

beats.say: Now we have both sides, 12 and 8. Which sum gives the area?
Area is length times breadth. 12 times 8 is 96.
So the area is 96 square centimetres.
Check the walk round. 12 plus 8 is 20, and double 20 is 40. That is the perimeter we were given.
So: halve the perimeter to get length plus breadth, take away the side you know, then multiply the two sides. The trap is to treat the perimeter as if it were a side.
An angle and its supplement sit together on a straight line. We are told the supplement is 3 times as big as the angle. How big is the angle?
We do not know the angle, so let's give it a name: x. Then the supplement, which is 3 times as big, is 3 x.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Look at the drawing. x and 3 x lie along a straight line. So what do they add up to?
A straight line is a half turn, 180 degrees. So x, plus 3 x, equals 180.
1 x and 3 more x's make 4 x. So 4 x equals 180.

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 4, we divide by 4, on both sides.

beats.say: 4 x means 4 times x. How do we undo times 4?
Divide both sides by 4. To divide by 4, halve and halve again. Half of 180 is 90, and half of 90 is 45.
So x equals 45. The angle is 45 degrees.
Let's check. The supplement is 3 times 45, which is 135. And 45 plus 135 makes 180, a straight line. It works.
So when a question gives a link between an angle and its supplement, call the angle x, write both on a straight line, and make them add up to 180.
Here is a triangle whose sides are written with the letter a: 2 a plus 6, 3 a plus 5, and a plus 7. We are told a is 3, and we want the perimeter.

ask.ifNot: A number written right next to a letter means times. So 2 a is 2 times 3, not 23.

beats.say: Wherever we see a, we put 3. But first: what does 2 a mean when a is 3?
The first side is 2 times 3, plus 6. 2 times 3 is 6, and 6 plus 6 is 12 centimetres.
The second side is 3 times 3, plus 5. 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 plus 5 is 14 centimetres.
The third side is the easy one: 3 plus 7 is 10 centimetres. Now every side has a real length.

ask.ifNot: The walk goes along every side, and a triangle has 3 of them. So we add all 3 lengths.

beats.say: Perimeter is the walk all the way round the triangle. Which sum gives it?
Add them one at a time. 12 plus 14 is 26. Then 26 plus 10 is 36.
So the perimeter is 36 centimetres.
Here is another way to check. Add the letters first: the 3 sides together are 6 a plus 18. And 6 times 3, plus 18, is 36 too.
So: put the number in place of the letter to get each side, then add all the sides for the walk round.

board.text: Clock shows 11:00 a.m. Hour hand turns 165°.

beats.say: The clock shows 11 o'clock in the morning. Then the hour hand, the short one, turns through 165 degrees. What time is it now?

board.text: Hour hand: full turn = 360° in 12 hours

beats.say: Here is the key fact. The hour hand goes right round the clock face, one full turn, in 12 hours. And a full turn is 360 degrees.

ask.ifNot: 360 degrees are shared equally among 12 hours, so we divide 360 by 12. Dividing by 60 is for the minute hand.

beats.say: So how far does the hour hand turn in just 1 hour?
360 divided by 12 is 30. So every hour, the hour hand moves 30 degrees, from one number to the next.
Now, how many 30s are there in 165? 5 thirties make 150. That leaves 15 degrees over.

ask.ifNot: 30 degrees is a whole hour, and 15 is half of 30. So it is half an hour. The trap is to read 15 degrees as 15 minutes.

beats.say: The 150 degrees are 5 whole hours. What about the 15 degrees left over?
15 is half of 30, so it is half an hour, which is 30 minutes. Altogether the hand has moved for 5 hours and 30 minutes.
Now add that to 11 o'clock. 1 hour takes us to 12 noon, and 4 more hours take us to 4 in the afternoon.
Then the extra 30 minutes. The time is 4:30 in the afternoon.
So remember: the hour hand turns 30 degrees every hour. Divide the turn by 30 for the hours, and change what is left over into minutes.
We have an equilateral triangle with a side of 8 centimetres. A square has the same perimeter as the triangle. How long is the side of the square?

ask.ifNot: The walk goes along all 3 sides, so we add 8 three times. That is the same as 3 times 8.

beats.say: Equilateral means all 3 sides are equal. So every side of this triangle is 8 centimetres. Which sum gives the walk all the way round it?
3 sides of 8 centimetres: 3 times 8 is 24. The triangle's perimeter is 24 centimetres.
The square has the same perimeter. So the walk round the square is 24 centimetres too.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, not 3. So the 24 centimetres are shared into 4 equal parts.

beats.say: A square has equal sides, and together they make 24. So how long is one side?
24 shared among 4 equal sides: 24 divided by 4 is 6. The side of the square is 6 centimetres.
Check: 4 sides of 6 make 24, exactly the same walk as the triangle.
Notice that the same perimeter does not mean the same side. The square has more sides to share the walk, so each one is shorter: 6, not 8.
Here is a rectangle whose breadth is half of its length. The perimeter is 48 centimetres, and we want the area.
We do not know either side yet, so let's think in parts. Call the breadth 1 part. The length is twice as long, so it is 2 parts.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts, but that is only halfway round. The whole walk is 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 parts.

beats.say: Now walk all the way round the rectangle: a length, a breadth, another length, another breadth. How many parts is the whole walk?
The whole walk is 6 parts, and we know the walk is 48 centimetres. So 1 part is 48 divided by 6, which is 8 centimetres.
So the breadth, 1 part, is 8 centimetres. And the length, 2 parts, is 2 times 8, which is 16 centimetres.
Let's check the walk. 16 plus 8 is 24, and that is halfway. Double it: 24 plus 24 is 48. Just what we were told.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides is for the walk round the edge. Area is rows of little squares, so we multiply the length by the breadth.

beats.say: Now for the area, the space inside. Which sum gives it?
16 times 8 is easier in two pieces. Split the 16 into 10 and 6. First, 8 times 10 is 80.
And 8 times 6 is 48. Put the two pieces together: 80 plus 48 makes 128.
So the area is 128 square centimetres.
So when you know how the sides compare, think in parts. Find one part from the perimeter, then the sides, then the area.

board.text: Facing North-East. Turns left. Now facing West.

beats.say: A man is cycling towards the North-East. He turns to his left until he is cycling towards the West. How big was his turn?

ask.ifNot: Face North-East and lift your left arm. It points round towards North. That is the anticlockwise way, against the hands of a clock.

beats.say: First, which way round the compass is a turn to the left?
A left turn goes anticlockwise. Now, the compass has 8 points, spaced evenly round a full turn of 360 degrees. 360 divided by 8 is 45. So each step from one point to the next is 45 degrees.
Let's take the turn one step at a time. The first step to the left goes from North-East to North. That is 45 degrees.
The second step goes from North to North-West. Another 45 degrees, so 90 degrees so far.

ask.ifNot: A turn of 90 degrees only reaches North-West. West is one more step of 45 degrees further round.

beats.say: He is facing North-West now. But he needs to face West. What is his total turn going to be?
One more step, from North-West to West. 90 plus 45 is 135. That is 3 steps of 45 degrees.
So he turned 135 degrees to his left.
So for any turn on a compass: count the steps between the points, and each step is 45 degrees.
This rectangle has its sides written with letters. The length is 4 a plus 3 b, and the breadth is 3 a minus b. We want the perimeter.
Perimeter is the walk all the way round: 2 lengths and 2 breadths. So we add the length and the breadth, and then double.

choices: a's with a's, and b's with b's
ask.ifNot: a and b are different things, like apples and bananas. We can only add apples to apples, and bananas to bananas.

beats.say: First, the length plus the breadth. Which terms are we allowed to add together?
The a's first. 4 a plus 3 a makes 7 a.
Now the b's. Careful: minus b means take away 1 b. So 3 b take away 1 b leaves 2 b. One length and one breadth make 7 a plus 2 b.

choices: No, it is only halfway round
ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth are only 2 of the 4 sides. That is halfway round, so we still have to double it.

beats.say: Is 7 a plus 2 b the perimeter?
It is only halfway round, so we double it. The 2 multiplies both terms: 2 times 7 a is 14 a, and 2 times 2 b is 4 b.
So the perimeter is 14 a plus 4 b.
Let's test it with easy numbers. Say a is 1 and b is 1. Then the length is 7 and the breadth is 2, so the perimeter is 2 times 9, which is 18. And 14 plus 4 is 18 as well.
So with letters the method is the same as with numbers: add length and breadth, keeping a's with a's and b's with b's, and then double everything.
Here is a square piece of ground. The walk all the way round it, its perimeter, is 120 metres. We want its area.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides, and together they make 120. So one side is 120 shared into 4 equal parts.

beats.say: For the area we need the side, and we are not given it. But the perimeter is made of the sides. So how do we get one side from 120?
4 equal sides share the 120 metres. 120 divided by 4 is 30. So each side is 30 metres.

ask.ifNot: 30 times 4 takes us straight back to the perimeter. Area is the space inside: side times side.

beats.say: Now the area, the space inside the square. Which sum gives it?
Area of a square is side times side. 3 times 3 is 9, and the two zeros come along: 30 times 30 is 900.
So the area is 900 square metres.
Check the side: 4 times 30 is 120, the perimeter we were given.
So the chain is: perimeter, then side, then area. And notice the units: plain metres for the walk round, square metres for the space inside.

board.text: 1 g of seed for each sq. m. Seed = ? kg

beats.say: A field is 110 metres long and 70 metres wide. Every square metre of it needs 1 gram of grass seed. How much seed is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: Seed is spread over the ground inside the field, not along its fence. The ground inside is the area: length times breadth.

beats.say: The seed covers the ground inside the field, 1 gram on each square metre. So what do we need to find first?
We need the area. For 110 times 70, do 11 times 7 first, which is 77. Then the two zeros come along: 7700.
The field is 7700 square metres. At 1 gram for each square metre, that is 7700 grams of seed.

ask.ifNot: 1000 grams make 1 kilogram. A kilogram is much bigger than a gram, so there will be fewer of them: we divide by 1000.

beats.say: But the choices are in kilograms. How do we change grams into kilograms?
1000 grams make 1 kilogram, so we divide by 1000. Every digit moves 3 places to the right, and 7700 becomes 7.7.
So the field needs 7.7 kilograms of grass seed.
Check by going back: 7.7 times 1000 is 7700 grams, 1 for each square metre.
So: the area tells us how many square metres, and that tells us how many grams. The last step, changing the unit, is where the slips happen.
We have 3 statements about complementary and supplementary angles, and each one says always. A good way to test an always is to try it on a real angle. Let's pick 30 degrees.
The complement fits with our angle in a right angle, 90 degrees. The supplement fits with it on a straight line, 180 degrees.
So the complement of 30 is 90 take away 30, which is 60. And the supplement is 180 take away 30, which is 150.

ask.ifNot: 150 is bigger than 90. One example that breaks an always is enough: the first statement is not true.

board.text: A: supplement is always less than 90°

beats.say: The first statement says the supplement is always less than 90 degrees. Our supplement is 150. What does that tell us?
150 is more than 90, so the first statement is out. One example that breaks an always is enough.

board.text: B: complement of an acute angle is acute

beats.say: The second statement says the complement of an acute angle is always acute. Acute means less than 90. Our 30 is acute, and its complement, 60, is acute too.

But is it always so? Look at the drawing: the two angles share one square corner of 90 degrees. A piece of the corner is always smaller than the whole corner, so the complement is always less than 90.
The third statement says the complement and the supplement always add up to 360. Ours are 60 and 150, and 60 plus 150 is 210. So that one is out as well.

board.text: True: complement of an acute angle is acute

beats.say: Only the second statement survives: the complementary angle of an acute angle is always an acute angle.
So when a statement says always, try it on a real angle. One example that breaks it is enough to throw it out. For the one that is left, look for the reason it must be true.
The perimeter of a rectangle is 72 centimetres. We have to pick the pair of numbers that could be its length and breadth.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth take us exactly halfway round. So together they make half of 72.

beats.say: The perimeter is the walk all the way round: 2 lengths and 2 breadths. So what must just one length and one breadth add up to?
Halfway round is half of 72, which is 36. So we are looking for a pair that adds up to 36.
Let's test each pair. 9 plus 4 is 13. And 14 plus 4 is 18. Neither of them is 36.
Next pair: 19 plus 15 is 34. Close, but not 36.
Last pair: 21 plus 15 is 36. That is the one.
So the length is 21 centimetres and the breadth is 15 centimetres.
Check the whole walk: 2 times 36 is 72. It fits.
The trap is to look for a pair that adds up to 72. Each side is walked twice, so the pair only has to make half of the perimeter.
Our angle is not a plain number this time. It is 38 minus x degrees, all in one bracket. We want its complementary angle.

ask.ifNot: A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Complementary angles fit together in a square corner, a right angle. So what do the two of them add up to?
A right angle is 90 degrees. So the partner is 90 take away our angle. And our angle is the whole bracket, so the whole bracket is taken away.

ask.ifNot: The angle is 38 with x already taken off, so it is smaller than 38. Take a smaller angle from 90 and more is left over. So the x comes back as plus x.

beats.say: Taking the bracket away takes away the 38. But what happens to the minus x inside?
Careful here: the minus in front of the bracket reaches both things inside. The 38 becomes minus 38, and the minus x becomes plus x.
Now tidy up. 90 take away 38 is 52. So we have 52 plus x.
So the complementary angle is 52 plus x degrees, written in a bracket.
Check by adding the two angles. The minus x and the plus x cancel, and 38 plus 52 is 90. A perfect right angle.
The slip to watch for is leaving the sign alone and writing 52 minus x. Taking away a bracket flips the signs inside it.
Two sides of a square are written with the letter a: 3 a minus 7, and 2 a minus 1. We want to know what its perimeter can be.

ask.ifNot: Every side of a square has the same length. So although they are written differently, these two sides are equal.

beats.say: The two sides look different. But this is a square. So what must be true about them?
All sides of a square are equal, so we can write an equation: 3 a minus 7 equals 2 a minus 1.
Let's clear the minus 7 first, by adding 7 to both sides. On the right, minus 1 plus 7 makes plus 6.
Now take 2 a away from both sides. 3 a take away 2 a leaves 1 a. So a equals 6.

choices: put it into 3a − 7 for the side
ask.ifNot: a is not the side. The side is 3 a minus 7, so we put 6 in place of a to find it.

beats.say: We know a is 6. What do we do with it next?
Put 6 in place of a. 3 times 6, minus 7, is 11. Check with the other side: 2 times 6, minus 1, is 11 too. So the side is 11 centimetres.
The perimeter is the walk round all 4 equal sides. 4 times 11 is 44.
So the perimeter is 44 centimetres.
So: equal sides give an equation, the equation gives a, a gives the side, and 4 sides give the perimeter. Do not stop at a.
The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is written with letters: 16 a plus 7 b. We are told a is 2 and b is 4, and we want one side.

ask.ifNot: A number written right next to a letter means times. So 16 a is 16 times 2.

beats.say: First we turn the perimeter into a real number. What does 16 a mean when a is 2?
16 a is 16 times 2, which is 32. And 7 b is 7 times 4, which is 28.
Add the two pieces. 32 plus 28 is 60. So the perimeter, the walk all the way round, is 60.

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all 3 sides of the triangle are equal. So the 60 is shared into 3 equal parts.

beats.say: Now, the triangle is equilateral. So how do we get one side from 60?
3 equal sides share the 60. 60 divided by 3 is 20. So each side is 20.
Check the walk: 20 plus 20 plus 20 makes 60. It fits.
So: put the numbers in place of the letters to get the perimeter, then share it among the 3 equal sides.
Here is a rectangle whose length is twice its breadth. The perimeter is 90 centimetres, and we want the area.
We do not know either side yet, so let's think in parts. Call the breadth 1 part. The length is twice as long, so it is 2 parts.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts, but that is only halfway round. The whole walk is 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 parts.

beats.say: Now walk all the way round the rectangle: a length, a breadth, another length, another breadth. How many parts is the whole walk?
The whole walk is 6 parts, and we know the walk is 90 centimetres. So 1 part is 90 divided by 6, which is 15 centimetres.
So the breadth, 1 part, is 15 centimetres. And the length, 2 parts, is 2 times 15, which is 30 centimetres.
Let's check the walk. 30 plus 15 is 45, and that is halfway. Double it: 45 plus 45 is 90. Just what we were told.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides is for the walk round the edge. Area is rows of little squares, so we multiply the length by the breadth.

beats.say: Now for the area, the space inside. Which sum gives it?
30 times 15. Do 3 times 15 first: that is 45. Then make it 10 times bigger, and we have 450.
So the area is 450 square centimetres.
So: breadth 1 part, length 2 parts, the walk round 6 parts. One part from the perimeter gives both sides, and the sides give the area.

board.text: Supplement of an obtuse angle is always ...?

beats.say: Here is an obtuse angle on a straight line, with its supplementary angle beside it. What kind of angle will that partner always be?
First, the names. An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle, 90 degrees, but smaller than a straight line, 180 degrees.
And supplementary angles share a straight line, so the two of them make 180 degrees together.
Let's try a real one. Say the obtuse angle is 120 degrees. Its supplement is 180 take away 120, which is 60 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The line holds 180 degrees, which is 2 lots of 90. If one angle takes more than 90, there must be less than 90 left over.

beats.say: Now think about every obtuse angle. It takes up more than 90 of the 180 degrees on the line. So how much is left for its partner?
There is always less than 90 left. Even a huge obtuse angle like 170 degrees leaves 10 degrees, which is still less than 90.
And an angle that is less than 90 degrees has a name: an acute angle. So the supplement of an obtuse angle is always acute.
So on a straight line, a big angle always has a small partner. Obtuse goes with acute, and a right angle goes with a right angle.
Our angle is not a plain number this time. It is 35 minus x degrees, all in one bracket. We want its complementary angle.

ask.ifNot: A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Complementary angles fit together in a square corner, a right angle. So what do the two of them add up to?
A right angle is 90 degrees. So the partner is 90 take away our angle. And our angle is the whole bracket, so the whole bracket is taken away.

ask.ifNot: The angle is 35 with x already taken off, so it is smaller than 35. Take a smaller angle from 90 and more is left over. So the x comes back as plus x.

beats.say: Taking the bracket away takes away the 35. But what happens to the minus x inside?
Careful here: the minus in front of the bracket reaches both things inside. The 35 becomes minus 35, and the minus x becomes plus x.
Now tidy up. 90 take away 35 is 55. So we have 55 plus x.
So the complementary angle is 55 plus x degrees, written in a bracket.
Check by adding the two angles. The minus x and the plus x cancel, and 35 plus 55 is 90. A perfect right angle.
The slip to watch for is leaving the sign alone and writing 55 minus x. Taking away a bracket flips the signs inside it.

board.text: Square: side 15 cm. Rectangle: length 25 cm.

beats.say: A square has a side of 15 centimetres. A rectangle with a length of 25 centimetres has the same area. We want the difference between their perimeters.
Start with what we can find: the area of the square, side times side. For 15 times 15, split one 15 into 10 and 5. 15 times 10 is 150.
And 15 times 5 is 75. Together, 150 plus 75 makes 225. So the square's area is 225 square centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Area is length times breadth. So to get back from the area to the breadth, we divide by the length.

beats.say: The rectangle has the same area, 225, and its length is 25. How do we find its breadth?
225 divided by 25 is 9, because 9 times 25 is 225. So the breadth is 9 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 25 plus 9 is only one length and one breadth, which is halfway round. We have to double it for the whole walk.

beats.say: Now the rectangle's perimeter, the walk all the way round. Which sum gives it?
25 plus 9 is 34, and that is halfway. Double it: the rectangle's perimeter is 68 centimetres.
The square's perimeter is easier: 4 equal sides of 15. 4 times 15 is 60 centimetres.
The difference is 68 take away 60, which is 8 centimetres.
Here is something worth noticing. The two shapes cover the same space, but the long thin one has the longer edge. Same area does not mean same perimeter.

board.text: E = side of equilateral triangle, S = side of square

beats.say: E is the side of an equilateral triangle, and S is the side of a square. We have to find the pair where the two shapes have the same perimeter.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides, so its walk round is 4 times S. S times S would be the space inside, the area.

beats.say: The triangle has 3 equal sides, so its walk round is 3 times E. What is the walk round the square?
The square has 4 equal sides, so its perimeter is 4 times S. Now we test each pair.
First pair: E is 9 and S is 9. 3 times 9 is 27, but 4 times 9 is 36. Not equal.
Second pair: E is 8 and S is 9. 3 times 8 is 24, and the square is still 36. Not equal.

ask.ifNot: The triangle has only 3 sides to make the same walk that the square makes with 4. So each of the triangle's sides has to be longer.

beats.say: Notice something. The square has more sides to walk along. So for the two walks to match, which side has to be the longer one?
The triangle's side has to be longer. Try E is 12 and S is 10. 3 times 12 is 36, but 4 times 10 is 40. Close, but not equal.
Last pair: E is 16 and S is 12. 3 times 16 is 48, and 4 times 12 is 48. Equal!
So the perimeters are equal when E is 16 and S is 12.
So when the choices are given, write the rule for each shape, then test the pairs one by one until both sides match.
The 3 angles of this triangle are written with x. They are x, x plus 10, and 2 x minus 6. We want the greatest angle.

ask.ifNot: Tear the corners off a paper triangle and line them up. They make a straight line, a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: We cannot compare the angles until we know x. So what do we know about the 3 angles of any triangle?
The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees. So we add ours and set the total equal to 180.
Gather the x's: 1 x, another x, and 2 x make 4 x. Then the plain numbers: plus 10 and minus 6 together make plus 4.
Take 4 away from both sides. 180 take away 4 leaves 176.
Divide both sides by 4, by halving twice. Half of 176 is 88, and half of 88 is 44. So x equals 44.

choices: Not yet: work out all 3 angles
ask.ifNot: x is only one of the angles. We have to work out the other two before we can say which is the greatest.

beats.say: x is 44. Is 44 degrees the greatest angle?
The first angle is 44 degrees. The second is 44 plus 10, which is 54 degrees. The third is 2 times 44, minus 6, which is 82 degrees.
Check that they make a triangle: 44 plus 54 plus 82 is 180. Good.
The angles are 44, 54 and 82 degrees. So the greatest angle is 82 degrees.
Careful with the last angle: 2 times 44 is 88, but we still have to take away the 6. So: angles add up to 180, find x, then work out every angle.

board.text: Right-angled triangle: sides 9 cm, 40 cm, 41 cm

beats.say: Here is a right-angled triangle. Its 3 sides are 9 centimetres, 40 centimetres and 41 centimetres. We want its area.

ask.ifNot: The longest side, 41, is the slanting one, opposite the right angle. The two shorter sides, 9 and 40, make the square corner.

beats.say: For the area we need a base, and a height that stands straight up from it, at a right angle. So which two sides meet at the right angle?
The two shorter sides make the right angle. So the base is 40 and the height is 9. Now watch: I draw a rectangle around the triangle, 40 long and 9 tall.
The rectangle's area is base times height. 4 times 9 is 36, so 40 times 9 is 360.

ask.ifNot: Our triangle is only half of the rectangle. So we need half of 360.

beats.say: The slanting side cuts that rectangle into two equal triangles. So what is the area of ours?
The triangle is half of the rectangle. Half of 360 is 180. That is the rule: half of base times height.
So the area is 180 square centimetres.
Notice that we never used the 41. The longest side is not a base or a height here, so it plays no part in the area. And do not forget the half.
Here the angle is written with a letter: x minus 35 degrees. We need the angle that is complementary to it.

ask.ifNot: A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Complementary angles fit together in a square corner, a right angle. So what do the two of them add up to?
A right angle is 90 degrees. So the partner is 90 take away our angle. And our angle is the whole bracket, so the whole bracket is taken away.

ask.ifNot: The angle is x with 35 already taken off. Taking away an angle that is 35 smaller leaves 35 more. So the 35 comes back as plus 35.

beats.say: Taking the bracket away takes away the x. But what happens to the minus 35 inside?
Careful here: the minus in front of the bracket reaches both things inside. The x becomes minus x, and the minus 35 becomes plus 35.
Now tidy up. 90 plus 35 is 125. So we have 125 minus x.
So the complementary angle is 125 minus x degrees, written in a bracket.
Check by adding the two angles. The x and the minus x cancel, and 125 take away 35 is 90. A perfect right angle.
The slip to watch for is leaving the sign alone. Taking away a bracket flips the signs inside it, so minus 35 turns into plus 35.

board.text: Right-angled triangle: sides 7 cm, 24 cm, 25 cm

beats.say: Here is a right-angled triangle with sides of 7, 24 and 25 centimetres. This time we are not asked for the area itself, but for a calculation that gives it.

ask.ifNot: The longest side, 25, is the slanting one, opposite the right angle. The two shorter sides, 7 and 24, make the square corner.

beats.say: The area needs a base, and a height standing straight up from it. So which two sides meet at the right angle?
The two shorter sides make the right angle, so they are the base and the height. Draw the rectangle around the triangle: the triangle is exactly half of it.
So the area is half of base times height: a half, times 24, times 7.

ask.ifNot: The half is used only once. Halve the 24 to get 12, and leave the 7 alone.

beats.say: We can do the half straight away, on the 24. So which of these is the same calculation?
Half of 24 is 12, so the area is 12 times 7. And 12 times 7 is the same as 7 times 12.
So the calculation is 7 times 12.
7 times 12 is 84 square centimetres. Look at the traps. 3.5 times 12 halves twice and gives only 42. And the 25 should never appear: the slanting side is neither base nor height.
So for a right-angled triangle: the two sides at the right angle are base and height, and the area is half of their product. Halve once, and only once.

board.text: Second: same area, length 16 cm. Width = ?

beats.say: The first rectangle is 12 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide. A second rectangle has the same area, but it is 16 centimetres long. How wide is it?

ask.ifNot: The two rectangles have the same area, so the area is the bridge from the first one to the second.

beats.say: The two rectangles share one thing. So what should we work out first?
The area of the first rectangle is length times width. 12 times 8 is 96 square centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Area is length times width. So to get back from the area to the width, we divide by the length. Adding 4 to one side and taking 4 off the other does not keep the area the same.

beats.say: The second rectangle also covers 96 square centimetres, and it is 16 long. How do we find its width?
96 divided by 16 is 6, because 16 times 6 is 96. So the width is 6 centimetres.
So the second rectangle is 6 centimetres wide.
Notice what happened. The length grew from 12 to 16, so the width had to shrink from 8 to 6 to hold the same area. Same area: multiply for the first, divide for the second.
Here the angle is written with a letter: 25 minus y degrees. We need the angle that is complementary to it.

ask.ifNot: A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Complementary angles fit together in a square corner, a right angle. So what do the two of them add up to?
A right angle is 90 degrees. So the partner is 90 take away our angle. And our angle is the whole bracket, so the whole bracket is taken away.

ask.ifNot: The angle is 25 with y already taken off, so it is smaller than 25. Take a smaller angle from 90 and more is left over. So the y comes back as plus y.

beats.say: Taking the bracket away takes away the 25. But what happens to the minus y inside?
Careful here: the minus in front of the bracket reaches both things inside. The 25 becomes minus 25, and the minus y becomes plus y.
Now tidy up. 90 take away 25 is 65. So we have 65 plus y.
So the complementary angle is 65 plus y degrees, written in a bracket.
Check by adding the two angles. The minus y and the plus y cancel, and 25 plus 65 is 90. A perfect right angle.
The slip to watch for is leaving the sign alone and writing 65 minus y. Taking away a bracket flips the signs inside it.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 96 cm, breadth = length − 6 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of a rectangle is 96 centimetres, and its breadth is 6 centimetres less than its length. We want the area.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth take us exactly halfway round. So together they are half of 96.

beats.say: The perimeter is the walk all the way round: 2 lengths and 2 breadths. So what do one length and one breadth add up to?
Half of 96 is 48. So the length and the breadth together make 48 centimetres.
Now picture the two sides as bars. The breadth bar is 6 short of the length bar. If we give the breadth that extra 6, we have two equal bars, and together they make 48 plus 6, which is 54.

ask.ifNot: With the extra 6 added, there are two bars of the same size making 54. So one of them is half of 54.

beats.say: Two equal bars make 54, and each one is as long as the length. So what is the length?
Half of 54 is 27, so the length is 27 centimetres. The breadth is 6 less: 27 take away 6 is 21 centimetres.
Check before going on: 27 plus 21 is 48, just as it should be.
27 times 21 is easier in two pieces. Split the 21 into 20 and 1. First, 27 times 20 is 540.
And 27 times 1 is 27. Put the two pieces together: 540 plus 27 makes 567.
So the area is 567 square centimetres.
The trap is to halve 48 and call both sides the same. They are not equal: one is 6 longer. So deal with the difference first, then halve.
Mishti is facing South-West. She turns 180 degrees clockwise, and then 225 degrees anticlockwise. Which way is she facing at the end?

choices: a quarter of the way round
ask.ifNot: A half turn spins you round to face exactly the other way. It does not even matter which way you turn.

beats.say: We take one turn at a time. The first turn is 180 degrees, which is a half turn. Where does a half turn leave you facing?
A half turn leaves her facing the opposite way. The opposite of South-West is North-East.
Now the second turn, 225 degrees. The compass has 8 points, spaced evenly round a full turn of 360 degrees. So each step from one point to the next is 45 degrees.
How many steps of 45 make 225? 5 times 45 is 225. So she turns 5 steps.

ask.ifNot: Clockwise from North goes to North-East and then East. Anticlockwise is the other way round, so from North-East she goes back towards North.

beats.say: Those 5 steps are anticlockwise. Starting from North-East, which way does anticlockwise take her first?
Count 5 steps anticlockwise from North-East: North, North-West, West, South-West, South.
So Mishti is facing South.
Here is a quick check. 180 one way and 225 back the other way leaves just 45 degrees anticlockwise. And 1 step anticlockwise from South-West is South.
So for turning questions: take one turn at a time, and count in steps of 45 degrees round the compass.
The sides of this triangle are written with the letter a: 3 a plus 5, 7 a plus 10, and 4 a plus 15. When a is 5, what is the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: A number written right next to a letter means times. So 7 a is 7 times 5, not 75.

beats.say: Wherever we see a, we put 5. But first: what does 7 a mean when a is 5?
The first side is 3 times 5, plus 5. 3 times 5 is 15, and 15 plus 5 is 20.
The second side is 7 times 5, plus 10. 7 times 5 is 35, and 35 plus 10 is 45.
The third side is 4 times 5, plus 15. 4 times 5 is 20, and 20 plus 15 is 35. Now every side has a real length.

ask.ifNot: The walk goes along every side, and a triangle has 3 of them. So we add all 3 lengths.

beats.say: Perimeter is the walk all the way round the triangle. Which sum gives it?
Add them one at a time. 20 plus 45 is 65. Then 65 plus 35 is 100.
So the perimeter is 100 units.
Another way to check: add the letters first. The 3 sides together are 14 a plus 30. And 14 times 5, plus 30, is 100 too.
So: put the number in place of the letter to get each side, then add all 3 sides for the walk round.
The perimeter of a rectangle is 84 centimetres, and its breadth is half of its length. We want the length.
We do not know either side yet, so let's think in parts. Call the breadth 1 part. The length is twice as long, so it is 2 parts.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts, but that is only halfway round. The whole walk is 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 parts.

beats.say: Now walk all the way round the rectangle: a length, a breadth, another length, another breadth. How many parts is the whole walk?
The whole walk is 6 parts, and we know the walk is 84 centimetres. So 1 part is 84 divided by 6, which is 14 centimetres.
So the breadth, 1 part, is 14 centimetres. And the length, 2 parts, is 2 times 14, which is 28 centimetres.
Let's check the walk. 28 plus 14 is 42, and that is halfway. Double it: 42 plus 42 is 84. Just what we were told.
The question asks for the length. The length is 28 centimetres.
The trap here is 42. That is half the perimeter: the length and the breadth together, not the length alone.

board.text: Square: same perimeter. Area of square = ?

beats.say: A rectangle is 22 metres long and 16 metres wide. A square has the same perimeter as this rectangle. We want the area of the square.

ask.ifNot: 22 plus 16 is only one length and one breadth, which is halfway round. We double it for the whole walk.

beats.say: Start with the rectangle's perimeter, the walk all the way round it. Which sum gives it?
22 plus 16 is 38, and that is halfway. Double it: 2 times 38 is 76. The rectangle's perimeter is 76 metres.
The square has the same walk round, 76 metres, shared among 4 equal sides. To divide by 4, halve and halve again. Half of 76 is 38, and half of 38 is 19.

ask.ifNot: The square shares the rectangle's perimeter, not its area. Its own area is its side times its side.

beats.say: So each side of the square is 19 metres. Now, which sum gives the square's area?
The area of a square is side times side.
19 times 19 is easier in two pieces. Split the 19 into 10 and 9. First, 19 times 10 is 190.
And 19 times 9 is 171. Put the two pieces together: 190 plus 171 makes 361.
So the area is 361 square metres. Now look at the choices: 324, 400 and 484. Our 361 is not among them.
When your answer is not on the list, check the working before you decide. 4 times 19 is 76, so the side is right. So the answer is: none of these.
So: perimeter of the rectangle, then the side of the square, then its area. And trust careful working, even when the list of choices does not have it.

board.text: Clock shows 12:45 p.m. Hour hand turns 214°.

beats.say: The clock shows 12:45 in the afternoon. Then the hour hand, the short one, turns through 214 degrees. What time is it now?

board.text: Hour hand: full turn = 360° in 12 hours

beats.say: The hour hand goes once round the clock, a full turn of 360 degrees, in 12 hours. 360 divided by 12 is 30. So it turns 30 degrees every hour.

ask.ifNot: 30 degrees are spread over 60 minutes. 30 is half of 60, so each minute gets half a degree. 6 degrees a minute is the speed of the minute hand.

beats.say: An hour is 60 minutes, and in that time the hour hand moves 30 degrees. So how far does it move in 1 minute?

board.text: Hour hand: 30° an hour, 1° every 2 minutes

beats.say: It moves half a degree a minute. Put the other way round: each whole degree takes the hour hand 2 minutes.
Now, how many whole hours are in 214 degrees? 7 thirties make 210. That leaves 4 degrees over.

ask.ifNot: Each degree takes the hour hand 2 minutes. So 4 degrees take 4 times 2 minutes.

beats.say: The 210 degrees are 7 whole hours. How long do the last 4 degrees take?
4 degrees, at 2 minutes each, is 8 minutes. So the hand has been moving for 7 hours and 8 minutes.
Add the 7 hours first. 7 hours after 12:45 is 7:45 in the evening.
Then the 8 minutes. 45 plus 8 is 53. The time is 7:53 in the evening.
So for the hour hand: 30 degrees is an hour, and each leftover degree is 2 minutes. Find the hours, then the minutes, then add them to the starting time.
Here is a right-angled triangle. We are not told its base or its height. We only know that its area is 18 times its base. We want the height.
We do know the rule for the area of any triangle: half of base times height. It is half of the rectangle drawn around it.
So now we have the same area written in two ways. They must be equal.

ask.ifNot: Both sides are something times the base. For them to be equal, the somethings must be equal: half of the height on the left, and 18 on the right.

beats.say: Look at both sides. Each one is something, times the base. What does that tell us?
The times base is on both sides, so we can cancel it from both. What is left is: half of the height equals 18.

ask.ifNot: If half of something is 18, the whole thing is twice as much. So we double 18.

beats.say: Half of the height is 18. So how do we get the whole height?
Double 18 is 36. So the height is 36 units.
Let's test it with a base of 10. Half of 10 times 36 is 180. And 18 times 10 is 180 too. It works.
So when the same thing multiplies both sides, cancel it. The trap here is to halve 18. Half of the height is 18, so the height itself is double.

board.text: Triangle: two sides 16 cm and 7 cm

beats.say: Two sides of a triangle are 16 centimetres and 7 centimetres. We do not know the third side, but we have to say what the perimeter could be.
The third side cannot be just anything. Picture the 7 side as a door, hinged to one end of the 16 side. Swing it wide open, flat, and the far ends are 16 plus 7 apart: 23.
Swing the door shut, flat against the 16 side, and the gap between the far ends is 16 take away 7: 9.

choices: No: the triangle would be flat
ask.ifNot: At exactly 23 or exactly 9 the door lies flat along the line, and there is no triangle left. The third side has to be in between.

beats.say: Can the third side be exactly 23, or exactly 9?
So the third side is more than 9 and less than 23. That is true for every triangle: more than the difference of the other two sides, less than their sum.
Now the perimeter. The two known sides make 23. Add the smallest and the largest third side: 23 plus 9 is 32, and 23 plus 23 is 46.

ask.ifNot: 31 is below 32. And 46 is the flat edge itself, which is not allowed. Only 34 lies properly in between.

beats.say: The choices are 34, 31 and 46. Which one lies between 32 and 46?
34 is between 32 and 46. It gives a third side of 34 take away 23, which is 11, safely between 9 and 23.
So a possible perimeter is 34 centimetres.
Remember the door. The third side of a triangle is always less than the sum of the other two, and more than their difference.
We are given 4 pairs of angles, all with decimals. We have to find the pair that is supplementary.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Supplementary angles fit together on a straight line, like this. So what must the pair add up to?

board.text: Supplementary: the pair adds up to 180°

beats.say: The pair must make exactly 180 degrees. So we add each pair. Here is a tip: look at the decimal parts first.
First pair: 127.5 and 53.5. The two point 5s make 1 whole, and the total comes to 181. One too many.
Second pair: 83.6 and 95.4. Point 6 and point 4 make 1 whole, and the total is 179. One short.
Third pair: 111.8 and 68.2. Point 8 and point 2 make 1 whole, and this time the total is exactly 180.
Check the last pair too: 115.7 and 65.3 make 181. So only one pair works.
The supplementary pair is 111.8 degrees and 68.2 degrees.
Notice how close the other pairs came: 179 and 181. Supplementary means exactly 180, so add carefully, decimals and all.

board.text: Square: side 56 cm. Rectangle: breadth 49 cm.

beats.say: A square has a side of 56 centimetres. A rectangle with a breadth of 49 centimetres has the same area. We want the perimeter of the rectangle.
The area of the square is side times side: 56 times 56. That comes to 3136 square centimetres, a big number. Keep it as 56 times 56 for a moment.

ask.ifNot: Area is length times breadth. So to get back from the area to the length, we divide by the breadth.

beats.say: The rectangle has that same area, and its breadth is 49. How do we find its length?
So the length is 56 times 56, divided by 49. Here is a neat way to do it. 49 is 7 times 7, and 56 is in the 7 times table: 56 divided by 7 is 8.
So divide each 56 by one of the 7s. We are left with 8 times 8, which is 64. The length is 64 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 64 plus 49 is only one length and one breadth, which is halfway round. We double it for the whole walk.

beats.say: Now the perimeter of the rectangle, the walk all the way round. Which sum gives it?
64 plus 49 is 113, and that is halfway. Double it: 2 times 113 is 226 centimetres.
Now look at the choices: 230, 224 and 222. Our 226 is not among them. Check the length before deciding: 64 times 49 is 3136, the same as the square. So it is right.
So the answer is: none of these.
So: the square's area, then the rectangle's length, then its perimeter. And when careful working gives an answer that is not on the list, none of these is the one to pick.

board.text: Clock at 7:20. Angle between the hands = ?

beats.say: The clock shows 7:20. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.
Here is the plan. We measure how far each hand has turned from the 12 at the top, one hand at a time. The whole clock face is a full turn, 360 degrees.
The minute hand first. It goes all the way round, 360 degrees, in 60 minutes. That is 6 degrees every minute. So at 20 minutes it has turned 20 times 6, which is 120 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand never stops. By 20 minutes past, it has crept on from the 7 towards the 8.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. At 7:20, where exactly is it pointing?
It is a little past the 7. Take the 7 first. Each hour is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees. So from the 12 round to the 7 is 7 times 30, which is 210 degrees.
Now the creep. The hour hand moves 30 degrees in 60 minutes, so half a degree each minute. In 20 minutes that is 10 degrees more. The hour hand is at 220 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The angle between the hands is the gap between their two positions, so we subtract. And we use 220, not 210, because the hour hand has moved past the 7.

beats.say: The minute hand is at 120 degrees and the hour hand is at 220 degrees. How do we get the angle between them?
220 take away 120 is 100. The angle between the hands is 100 degrees.
So work the two hands separately: 6 degrees a minute for the minute hand, 30 degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute for the hour hand. Forget the creep, and you are 10 degrees out.

board.text: Rectangle: same perimeter. L and B = ?

beats.say: An equilateral triangle has a side of 12 centimetres. A rectangle has the same perimeter as the triangle. We have to pick the length and breadth it could have.

ask.ifNot: The walk goes along all 3 sides, so we add 12 three times. That is the same as 3 times 12.

beats.say: Equilateral means all 3 sides are equal. Which sum gives the walk all the way round the triangle?
3 times 12 is 36. The triangle's perimeter is 36 centimetres, and so is the rectangle's.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth take us exactly halfway round. So together they make half of 36.

beats.say: The walk round a rectangle is 2 lengths and 2 breadths. So what must one length and one breadth add up to?
Half of 36 is 18. So we are looking for a pair that adds up to 18.
Test the pairs. 10 plus 5 is 15: too small. 14 plus 6 is 20: too big.
8 plus 6 is 14: too small. And 13 plus 5 is 18. That is the one.
So the rectangle can have a length of 13 centimetres and a breadth of 5 centimetres.
Check the whole walk: 2 times 18 is 36, the same as the triangle.
The trap is to look for a pair that makes 36. Each side of a rectangle is walked twice, so the pair only makes half of the perimeter.

board.text: Sides become 5/4 and 3/5 of 30. Area difference = ?

beats.say: A square has a side of 30 centimetres. One side is stretched to 5 quarters of its length, and another is shrunk to 3 fifths. That makes a rectangle. How different are the two areas?
The square's area first. Side times side: 3 times 3 is 9, so 30 times 30 is 900 square centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 4 quarters make the whole. 5 quarters is one quarter more than the whole, so it is bigger than 30.

beats.say: Now the stretched side: 5 quarters of 30. Before we work it out, will it be bigger or smaller than 30?
It is bigger. One quarter of 30 is 30 divided by 4, which is 7.5. So 5 quarters is 5 times 7.5, which is 37.5 centimetres.
Now the shrunk side: 3 fifths of 30. One fifth of 30 is 6, so 3 fifths is 3 times 6, which is 18 centimetres.
The rectangle's area is 37.5 times 18. Here is a neat trick: double one number and halve the other, and the product stays the same. So it is 75 times 9.
75 times 9: 70 times 9 is 630, and 5 times 9 is 45. Together that is 675 square centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Difference means how much bigger one is than the other. So we take the smaller area away from the larger one.

beats.say: The square covers 900 and the rectangle covers 675. Which sum gives the difference?
900 take away 675 is 225. The difference is 225 square centimetres.
So: find each new side, then each area, then subtract. One side grew and one shrank, but the area did not stay the same.
Shraddha is facing East. She turns 135 degrees clockwise, and then 315 degrees anticlockwise. Which way is she facing at the end?
The compass has 8 points, spaced evenly round a full turn of 360 degrees. 360 divided by 8 is 45. So each step from one point to the next is 45 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Clockwise from East goes to South-East, then South, then South-West. Count all 3 steps.

beats.say: The first turn is 135 degrees, and 3 times 45 is 135. So it is 3 steps clockwise from East. Where does that take her?
South-East, South, South-West. After the first turn she is facing South-West.
Now the second turn: 315 degrees anticlockwise. That is a big one, nearly a full turn. How far short of a full turn is it? 360 take away 315 is 45.

ask.ifNot: She is turning anticlockwise and stops before she gets all the way back. So she is still 45 degrees on the clockwise side of South-West.

beats.say: A full turn would bring her right back to South-West. She stops 45 degrees short of that. So where does she end up, compared with South-West?
So turning 315 degrees anticlockwise ends in the same place as turning 45 degrees clockwise. And 1 step clockwise from South-West is West.
So Shraddha is facing West.
So take one turn at a time, in steps of 45 degrees. And for a very big turn, it is quicker to ask how far short of a full turn it is.
A circle has an area of 616 square centimetres. Its circumference is the same as the perimeter of a square. We want the area of that square.

board.text: Area of circle = π × r × r, with π = 22/7

beats.say: It is a chain: the circle's area gives its radius, the radius gives the circumference, and that gives the square. The area of a circle is pi times the radius times the radius, and for pi we use 22 over 7.
So 22 over 7, times r times r, is 616. To undo that, divide by 22 and multiply by 7. 616 divided by 22 is 28, and 28 times 7 is 196.

ask.ifNot: We need a number that multiplies by itself to make 196, not half of 196. 14 times 14 is 196.

beats.say: r times r is 196. So what is r?
14 times 14 is 196, so the radius is 14 centimetres.
Now the circumference, the walk round the circle: 2 times pi times the radius. 14 divided by 7 is 2, so it is 2 times 22 times 2, which is 88 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides, and together they make 88. So one side is 88 shared into 4 equal parts.

beats.say: The square's perimeter is the same: 88 centimetres. How do we get one side of the square?
88 divided by 4 is 22. Each side of the square is 22 centimetres.
Last step: the square's area, side times side. 22 times 20 is 440, and 22 times 2 is 44. Together that makes 484.
So the area of the square is 484 square centimetres.
A long chain, but each link is small: area to radius, radius to circumference, circumference to side, side to area. Write each link down before starting the next.

board.text: Clock at 9:33. Angle between the hands = ?

beats.say: The clock shows 9:33. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.
We measure how far each hand has turned from the 12 at the top, one hand at a time. The whole clock face is a full turn, 360 degrees.
The minute hand first. It goes all the way round, 360 degrees, in 60 minutes, so it turns 6 degrees every minute.
At 33 minutes it has turned 33 times 6. 30 times 6 is 180, and 3 times 6 is 18. Together, 198 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand never stops. 33 minutes is a little more than half an hour, so the hand is a little more than halfway from the 9 to the 10.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. At 9:33, where exactly is it pointing?
Take the 9 first. Each hour is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees. So from the 12 round to the 9 is 9 times 30, which is 270 degrees.
Now the creep. The hour hand moves 30 degrees in 60 minutes, so half a degree each minute. In 33 minutes that is half of 33, which is 16.5 degrees.
So the hour hand is at 270 plus 16.5, which is 286.5 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The angle between the hands is the gap between their two positions, so we subtract. And we use 286.5, not 270, because the hour hand has moved past the 9.

beats.say: The hour hand is at 286.5 degrees and the minute hand is at 198 degrees. How do we get the angle between them?
To take away 198, take away 200 and then give 2 back. 286.5 take away 200 is 86.5, and 2 more makes 88.5.
The angle between the hands is 88.5 degrees.
So work the two hands separately: 6 degrees a minute for the minute hand, and 30 degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute for the hour hand. Then subtract.
A rectangle has an area of 468 square centimetres, and its breadth is 18 centimetres. We want its perimeter.

ask.ifNot: Area is length times breadth. So to get back from the area to the length, we divide by the breadth.

beats.say: For the perimeter we need both sides, and we only have the breadth. The area will give us the length. How?
We need 468 divided by 18: how many 18s make 468? Start with a big chunk. 20 lots of 18 make 360. That leaves 468 take away 360, which is 108.
And 6 lots of 18 make 108. So altogether that is 20 lots and 6 lots: 26. The length is 26 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 26 plus 18 is only one length and one breadth, which is halfway round. We double it for the whole walk.

beats.say: Now the perimeter, the walk all the way round. Which sum gives it?
26 plus 18 is 44, and that is halfway. Double it: 2 times 44 is 88.
So the perimeter is 88 centimetres.
Check the length by multiplying back: 26 times 18 is 468, the area we were given.
So: divide the area by the side you know to find the other side, then add the two sides and double.
Our angle is 58 degrees. It has two partners: a complementary angle and a supplementary angle. We want the two partners added together.

ask.ifNot: A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line, which comes next.

beats.say: Take the complementary angle first. It fits with 58 degrees inside a square corner, a right angle. So what do the two of them make together?
A right angle is 90 degrees. So the complementary angle is 90 take away 58.
Let's take 58 away in two easy hops. First the 50: 90 take away 50 leaves 40.
